title: Light & Optics
description: How light behaves — reflection, refraction, lenses, the eye, colour, dispersion, and ray diagrams.

notes.heading: Light as a Wave
notes.body: Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave that travels at 3×10⁸ m/s in a vacuum. It does not need a medium — it can travel through empty space. Light travels in straight lines (rays). When light hits an object, it can be: reflected (bounces off), refracted (bends entering new medium), absorbed (energy taken in), or transmitted (passes through). Opaque objects absorb/reflect light — you cannot see through them. Transparent objects transmit light — you can see through clearly (glass, clear plastic). Translucent objects transmit light but scatter it — you see light but not a clear image (frosted glass, wax paper). Shadows form when light is blocked by an opaque object. A point source creates a sharp shadow (umbra); an extended source creates a fuzzy edge (penumbra).

notes.heading: Reflection and Mirrors
notes.body: Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection, both measured from the NORMAL (a line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence). Specular reflection: smooth surface → parallel incident rays reflected as parallel rays → clear image (mirror, calm water). Diffuse reflection: rough surface → parallel rays scattered in all directions → no image, just brightness (paper, wall — this is how we see non-shiny objects). Plane mirror: image is virtual (cannot be projected on screen), upright, same size as object, laterally inverted (left-right swapped), same distance behind mirror as object is in front. Ray diagrams: draw at least two rays from object to locate image. Incident ray hits mirror → reflected at equal angle. Extend reflected rays back behind mirror (dashed lines for virtual rays) — they meet at the image location.

notes.heading: Refraction and Snell's Law
notes.body: Refraction: light bends when crossing a boundary between media of different optical densities at an angle. This happens because light changes speed. Entering a denser medium (air → glass/water): light slows down → bends TOWARDS the normal. Entering a less dense medium (glass → air): speeds up → bends AWAY from the normal. Along the normal (0° angle): no change in direction, only speed. Snell's Law: n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂, where n is the refractive index. Refractive index = speed of light in vacuum ÷ speed in medium. Diamond: n≈2.42 (light slows dramatically → lots of refraction → sparkle). Water: n≈1.33. Total internal reflection: when light in a denser medium hits the boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle, it reflects entirely back — no transmission. This is how optical fibres work (communications, endoscopes). Critical angle equation: sin c = 1/n. Applications: fibre optic internet, medical imaging (endoscopy), diamond brilliance.

notes.heading: Convex and Concave Lenses
notes.body: Lenses refract light to form images. Convex lens (converging): thicker in middle. Parallel rays converge at the focal point (F). Focal length (f): distance from lens centre to focal point. Ray diagram rules: (1) Ray parallel to axis → passes through F on other side. (2) Ray through centre of lens → continues straight. (3) Ray through F on the way in → emerges parallel to axis. Image properties depend on object distance: Object beyond 2F → real, inverted, diminished (camera). Object at 2F → real, inverted, same size. Object between F and 2F → real, inverted, magnified (projector). Object at F → no image (rays parallel, image at infinity). Object inside F → virtual, upright, magnified (magnifying glass). Real images can be projected on screen; virtual images cannot. Concave lens (diverging): thinner in middle. Always produces virtual, upright, diminished image. Used for correcting short-sightedness (myopia).

notes.heading: The Human Eye and Vision Defects
notes.body: The eye is a biological optical system: Cornea — transparent front, does most of the focusing. Pupil — hole letting light in; iris controls size. Lens — fine-tunes focus by changing shape (accommodation). Retina — light-sensitive layer (rods — dim light; cones — colour). Optic nerve — carries signals to brain. Short-sightedness (myopia): image focuses in FRONT of retina. Cannot see distant objects clearly. Caused by eyeball too long or cornea too curved. Corrected with concave (diverging) lens. Long-sightedness (hyperopia): image focuses BEHIND retina. Cannot see near objects clearly. Caused by eyeball too short or lens loses flexibility (age). Corrected with convex (converging) lens. The near point of a normal eye is ~25 cm. The far point is infinity. Power of a lens (dioptres, D) = 1/f (f in metres). Concave lens: negative power. Convex lens: positive power.

notes.heading: Colour, Dispersion and Filters
notes.body: White light is a mixture of all visible wavelengths (~400-700 nm). Dispersion: splitting white light into ROYGBIV spectrum using a prism. Violet refracts most (shortest λ, slowest in glass); red refracts least (longest λ, fastest). Additive colour mixing (light): primary = Red, Green, Blue. R+G=Yellow, R+B=Magenta, G+B=Cyan, R+G+B=White. Used in screens (RGB pixels). Subtractive colour mixing (pigments/paints): primary = Cyan, Magenta, Yellow. C+M+Y = Black (K). Used in printing (CMYK). Why a red apple looks red: (1) White light shines on apple. (2) Apple surface absorbs all colours EXCEPT red. (3) Red light is reflected to your eyes. A white object reflects ALL colours; a black object absorbs ALL colours (heats up most). Filters: red filter transmits ONLY red, absorbs green and blue. Shine white light through red filter → only red passes. Shine blue light through red filter → nothing (blue absorbed, red filter blocks it). Colour perception is about which wavelengths reach your eye.

notes.heading: Practical Optics and Visible Light
notes.body: Visible light is just a tiny slice of the EM spectrum. Applications of lenses and mirrors: Periscopes (two mirrors at 45° → see over obstacles), telescopes (refracting: lenses; reflecting: mirrors — gather faint light from distant objects), microscopes (two convex lenses in series → high magnification), cameras (lens focuses image onto sensor/film — aperture controls light; shutter controls time). Magnification: M = image height ÷ object height. Also M = image distance ÷ object distance. The pinhole camera: simple model — tiny hole projects inverted, real image. Smaller hole = sharper but dimmer image (diffraction limits). Larger hole = brighter but blurrier. Optical fibres: thin glass/plastic strands using total internal reflection to transmit light signals over long distances with minimal loss — backbone of the internet (submarine cables).

flashcards.definition: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection, measured from the NORMAL.
flashcards.example: Ray hits mirror at 30° to normal → reflected at 30°.

flashcards.definition: Light bends when crossing boundary between media of different density due to speed change.
flashcards.example: Pencil appears bent in water — light from submerged part refracts at water-air boundary.

flashcards.definition: Light in denser medium hits boundary at angle > critical angle → 100% reflected, zero transmitted.
flashcards.example: Optical fibres — light bounces along inside glass core, enabling high-speed data transmission.

flashcards.definition: Thicker in middle. Parallel rays converge at focal point. Can produce real or virtual images.
flashcards.example: Magnifying glass (object inside F → virtual, upright, magnified image).

flashcards.definition: Thinner in middle. Always produces virtual, upright, diminished image. Corrects short-sightedness.
flashcards.example: Glasses for myopia — diverging lens spreads light before it enters the eye.

flashcards.definition: Distance from lens centre to focal point. Determines lens power. Shorter f = stronger lens.
flashcards.example: Lens power (dioptres) = 1/f(m). f=0.5 m → 2 D. f=0.1 m → 10 D.

flashcards.definition: Real: light rays actually converge — can project on screen. Virtual: rays only appear to meet — cannot project.
flashcards.example: Projector → real image. Mirror → virtual image.

flashcards.definition: Image focuses IN FRONT of retina. Can't see distant objects. Corrected with concave lens.
flashcards.example: Myopic person squints to see distant road signs clearly.

flashcards.definition: Image focuses BEHIND retina. Can't see near objects. Corrected with convex lens.
flashcards.example: Long-sighted person holds book at arm's length to read.

flashcards.definition: Splitting white light into ROYGBIV by refraction. Violet bends most; red bends least.
flashcards.example: Rainbow — sunlight dispersed by water droplets. Pink Floyd album cover.

flashcards.definition: Red + Green + Blue = White. Screens use RGB pixels at different intensities to create all colours.
flashcards.example: Yellow on screen = R+G lit. Magenta = R+B lit.

flashcards.definition: The incident angle in denser medium above which total internal reflection occurs. sin c = 1/n.
flashcards.example: Glass (n=1.5): sin c=1/1.5=0.667 → c≈42°. Diamond (n=2.42): c≈24° — lots of TIR = sparkle.

questions.stem: Light hits a mirror at 35° to the normal. Angle of reflection?
questions.explanation: Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection = 35°.

questions.stem: Light travels from air (n≈1) into glass (n≈1.5). It will:
choices: Speed up, bend away from normal
questions.explanation: Entering denser medium → slower → bends TOWARDS the normal.

questions.stem: An object placed inside the focal point of a convex lens produces:
questions.explanation: Object distance < f → magnifying glass effect: virtual, upright, magnified image.

choices: Concave (diverging) — spreads light, moving focal point back onto retina
questions.explanation: Myopia: image focuses too early. Concave lens diverges rays, effectively lengthening focal length.

questions.stem: Why does a diamond sparkle more than glass?
choices: Higher refractive index (n≈2.42 vs 1.5) → lower critical angle (~24°) → more total internal reflection → more sparkle
questions.explanation: Small critical angle = light bounces around inside many times before escaping — creates brilliant sparkle.

questions.stem: A red filter in white light appears red because:
choices: It adds red to all light
It transmits red light and absorbs all other colours
It converts all light to red
questions.explanation: Filters transmit their own colour; absorb complementary colours.

choices: Virtual, upright, same size, laterally inverted
questions.explanation: Plane mirror: virtual (behind mirror), upright, laterally inverted, same distance behind as object is in front.

choices: Light in denser medium hitting boundary at angle > critical angle
questions.explanation: TIR: (1) light in denser medium, (2) angle > critical angle. Both conditions must be met.

questions.stem: Lens power: f=0.25 m. Power in dioptres?
questions.explanation: P=1/f=1/0.25=4 D. Shorter focal length = more powerful lens.

questions.stem: Object beyond 2F of convex lens produces:
questions.explanation: Object distance > 2F → real, inverted, diminished image. This is how cameras work.

questions.stem: A green leaf in red light appears:
choices: Black — leaf absorbs red (only reflects green); no green in red light → no light reflected = black
questions.explanation: A green object reflects only green light. Red light contains no green → leaf absorbs all red light → no light reflected → appears black.

questions.stem: Red + Green light on white screen produces:

choices: Total internal reflection — light bounces along the core without escaping
questions.explanation: TIR keeps light inside the fibre core, even around bends, enabling long-distance, low-loss data transmission.

questions.stem: When light enters glass at exactly 0° (along the normal):
choices: It continues straight — no change in direction, only speed
questions.explanation: No change in direction when entering along the normal. Speed changes but the ray path is unchanged.

questions.stem: A real image can be projected on a screen. What property must it have?
choices: Light rays from the object actually converge at the image location
It is always smaller than object
questions.explanation: Real image = light actually passes through the image point. Virtual image = light only appears to come from that point.
